<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:MorseFun}
 Let $\Lambda$ be a simplicial complex and let $f : \Lambda \to \mathbb{R}$ assign a real value to each simplex. For a $p$-simplex $\alpha \in \Lambda^p$, define
\begin{eqnarray}
    U_f(\alpha) &=&
\{\beta \in \Lambda^{p+1} \mid \alpha < \beta,\ f(\beta) \le f(\alpha)\}\\
V_f(\alpha)
&=&
\{\gamma \in \Lambda^{p-1} \mid \gamma < \alpha,\ f(\gamma) \ge f(\alpha)\}.\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}

The function $f$ is a \emph{discrete Morse function} if
$
|U_f(\alpha)| \le 1$ and
$|V_f(\alpha)| \le 1$ for all $\alpha \in \Lambda$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:CritSimp}
A simplex $\alpha$ is \emph{critical} if
                  
                       
$|U_f(\alpha)| = |V_f(\alpha)| = 0.$
                
Equivalently, all cofaces of $\alpha$ have strictly larger function values and all faces have strictly smaller values.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C}(f)$ be the set of critical cells for a graph $G$ with a set of vertices $V$ ($N = |V|$), set of edges $E$ ($M = |E|$), with clique complex $Cl(G)$ and some discrete Morse
function $f$. Rather than retaining the full descending manifold of each critical cell,
which may be large and unstable,                             
we associate to each $\alpha \in \mathcal{C}(f)$ a \emph{single representative
descending path} $\pi(\alpha)$ 
obtained by following a deterministic,
gradient-respecting walk in the directed Hasse diagram (see Appx.~\ref{sec:hasse} for more details.)                             
    Then, the            
    Morse skeleton (MS) is the finite set $S(G):=(\mathcal{C,D})= (\mathcal{C},\{ (\alpha, \pi(\alpha)) : \alpha \in \mathcal{C}(f) \}),
$
which encodes the essential information on both the locations of topological events (critical cells)
and a minimal, canonical description of how combinatorial flow propagates
from them.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:skel-strict-refinement}
Let $G = (V, E)$ be a graph equipped with a discrete Morse function $f$
and let $\mathcal{S}(G) = (E^{\mathrm{crit}}, E^{\mathrm{pair}})$ be its Morse skeleton with its associated gradient vector field $\mathcal{V}$.  Let
$\mathrm{Dgm}(G)$ be persistence diagram $\mathrm{Dgm}(G)$ of $G$ under sublevel
filtration of~$f$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Strict refinement.}
        $\mathcal{S}(G)$ determines $\mathrm{Dgm}(G)$, but the
        converse fails: there exist graphs $G, G'$ with
        $\mathrm{Dgm}(G) = \mathrm{Dgm}(G')$ and $\mathcal{S}(G) \neq \mathcal{S}(G')$.  In
        particular, the descending-manifold structure that defines
        our edge partition is not recoverable from $\mathrm{Dgm}(G)$.
  \item \textbf{Margin-based stability.}
        Under the no-ties condition, $\mathcal{S}(G)$ enjoys a
        \emph{computable} stability radius
          $r(s) = \frac{m(s)}{L_\Delta} > 0,$
        where $m(s)$ is the minimum decision-gap margin and
        $L_\Delta$ is the Lipschitz constant of the decision gaps:
        every data perturbation of magnitude strictly less than
        $r(s)$ leaves $\mathcal{S}(G)$ unchanged
        (See Appx. \ref{sec:stability_skeleton_guidance}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:decision_margin}
For a state $s$ in our extractor map $\mathbb{S}$, under no-ties condition, the \emph{decision margin} is $m(s) := \min_{j \in \mathcal{J}} |\Delta_j(s)|$, where $\mathcal{J}$ is a finite index set.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:margin_preserves_skel}
   Let $\mathrm{Skel} : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{S}$ be the skeleton extractor,
where $\mathbb{S}$ denotes the (finite) space of skeletons of $\mathrm{Cl}(G)$.
Assume $\mathrm{Skel}$ depends on the input only through a feature map
$\varphi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ and a finite set of strict scalar
comparisons: namely, there exist a finite index set $\mathcal{J}$, functions
$u_j, v_j : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, and a deterministic map
$F : \{-1, +1\}^{\mathcal{J}} \to \mathbb{S}$ such that for every state
$s \in \mathcal{S}$ satisfying the no-ties condition $\Delta_j(s) \neq 0$ for
all $j \in \mathcal{J}$, we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \mathrm{Skel}(s)=F\bigl((\mathrm{sign} (\Delta_j(s)))_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\bigr)  \quad \rm{and} \quad
\Delta_j(s):=u_j(\varphi(s))-v_j(\varphi(s)).
\end{eqnarray*}
Further assume the decision gaps are $\ell_\infty$-Lipschitz:                                                                                         
$$\exists L_\Delta<\infty, \quad \rm{such \,\ that} \quad |\Delta_j(s')-\Delta_j(s)|\le L_\Delta\|\varphi(s')-\varphi(s)\|_\infty, \qquad \forall j\in\mathcal{J}, \forall s,s'\in\mathbb{S}.$$                                                                  
Then, if decision margin $m(s)>0$ and
$\|\varphi(s')-\varphi(s)\|_\infty<m(s)/L_\Delta$,          
$\mathrm{Skel}(s')=\mathrm{Skel}(s)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Table~\ref{tab:forecasting} presents
results on graph diffusion for spatio-temporal forecasting.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-dimensional manifold and let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function. A point $p \in M$ is called a \emph{critical point} of $f$ if the differential of $f$ vanishes at $p$, i.e., $df_p = 0$. Equivalently, in any local coordinate chart $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ around $p$, all first partial derivatives vanish at $p$:
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(p) = 0 \quad \text{for all } i=1,\dots,n.
\]
A point $p$ is called a \emph{regular point} if $df_p \neq 0$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
A smooth function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{Morse function} if all of its critical points are non-degenerate. That is, for every $p \in M$ such that $\nabla f(p) = 0$, the Hessian $\mathrm{Hess}_p(f)$ is non-singular.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $p$ be a critical point of a Morse function $f$. The \emph{Morse index} of $p$, denoted $\operatorname{ind}(p)$, is the number of negative eigenvalues of $\mathrm{Hess}_p(f)$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
The \emph{descending manifold} of a critical point $p$ is
\[
W^s(p) = \{ x \in M \mid \lim_{t \to +\infty} \varphi_t(x) = p \}.
\]
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
The \emph{ascending manifold} of $p$ is
\[
W^u(p) = \{ x \in M \mid \lim_{t \to -\infty} \varphi_t(x) = p \}.
\]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Two closed $(d-1)$-manifolds $M_0$ and $M_1$ are \emph{cobordant} if there exists a $d$-manifold $W$ such that
\[
\partial W = M_0 \sqcup M_1.
\]
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
A function $f : \Lambda \to \mathbb{R}$ is called a \emph{discrete Morse function} if for every simplex $\alpha \in \Lambda^p$,
\begin{equation}
|U_f(\alpha)| \leq 1 \quad \text{and} \quad |V_f(\alpha)| \leq 1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
A simplex $\alpha \in K^p$ is said to be \emph{critical} if
\begin{equation}
|U_f(\alpha)| = |V_f(\alpha)| = 0.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $\alpha$ is critical if all cofaces $\beta$ of $\alpha$ satisfy $f(\beta) > f(\alpha)$ and all faces $\gamma$ of $\alpha$ satisfy $f(\gamma) < f(\alpha)$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:dgvf}
A \emph{discrete gradient vector field} $\mathcal{V}$ is a collection of pairs $(\alpha^{(p)},\beta^{(p+1)})$ with $\alpha\subset\beta$, such that each cell appears in at most one pair. We require $\mathcal{V}$ to be \emph{acyclic}, i.e., there are no nontrivial closed $\mathcal{V}$-paths.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:compatibility_notion}
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite cell complex, $f:\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}$ a discrete Morse function, and $\mathcal{V}$ a discrete gradient vector field.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{$f$-admissible (induced-filtration compatible).}
We say $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{$f$-admissible} if for every matched pair $(\sigma^{(p)},\tau^{(p+1)})\in\mathcal{V}$ we have
\[
f(\tau)\le f(\sigma).
\]
Equivalently, if $F_t:=\{\alpha\in \Lambda: f(\alpha)\le t\}$ is the sublevel-set filtration induced by $f$, then $\sigma\in F_t$ implies its paired coface (if any) also lies in $F_t$.

\item \textbf{Strict filtered matching (external filtration).}
Given an externally specified filtration $F:\Lambda_0\subset\cdots\subset \Lambda_T$ and entry time $t_F(\alpha)$, we say $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{entry-time compatible} if every matched pair satisfies $t_F(\sigma)=t_F(\tau)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:Vpath_general}
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite regular CW complex and let $\mathcal{V}$ be a discrete gradient vector field on $\Lambda$.
A \emph{$\mathcal{V}$-path} is a sequence of cells
\[
\sigma_0^{(p)} \prec \tau_0^{(p+1)} \succ \sigma_1^{(p)} \prec \tau_1^{(p+1)} \succ \cdots
\prec \tau_{m-1}^{(p+1)} \succ \sigma_m^{(p)}
\]
such that $(\sigma_i,\tau_i)\in\mathcal{V}$ for each $i$ and $\sigma_{i+1}$ is a codimension-$1$ face of $\tau_i$ with $\sigma_{i+1}\neq \sigma_i$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:descending_set}
Fix $\mathcal{V}$ on $\Lambda$. For a critical $p$-cell $\sigma$, define its \emph{descending set}
\[
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{V}}(\sigma)
:= \{\, \tau \in \Lambda \;:\; \text{ exists $\mathcal{V}$-path at $\sigma$ reaching $\tau$}\,\}.
\]
Equivalently, $\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{V}}(\sigma)$ if $\tau$ is reachable from $\sigma$ by repeatedly following the directed incidences induced by $\mathcal{V}$ in the Hasse diagram.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Many authors refer to $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{V}}(\sigma)$ as the \emph{discrete descending region} or \emph{descending manifold} (discrete unstable manifold). We use \emph{descending set} to emphasize that this is a combinatorial reachability object rather than a smooth submanifold.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:acyclic_graph}
The vector field $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{acyclic} if there is no nontrivial closed $\mathcal{V}$-path. Equivalently, there do not exist vertices $v_0,\dots,v_{k-1}$ and edges $e_0,\dots,e_{k-1}$ with $k\ge 1$ such that for each $i$ (indices mod $k$),
\[
(v_i,e_i)\in\mathcal{V}, \qquad e_i=\{v_i,v_{i+1}\},
\]
and $v_k=v_0$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def:Gamma_fullgraph}
Define the paired-edge set
\[
E^{\mathrm{pair}} := \{\, e\in E : \exists v\in V \text{ such that } (v,e)\in\mathcal{V}\,\}.
\]
For each paired edge $e=\{v,w\}\in E^{\mathrm{pair}}$, exactly one endpoint is paired to it; write $(v,e)\in\mathcal{V}$. Define a directed graph $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ on vertex set $V$ by adding the directed edge $v\to w$ for each such pair $(v,e)$.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:outdegree_bound}
Every vertex in $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ has outdegree at most $1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Each vertex appears in at most one pair $(v,e)\in\mathcal{V}$ by definition of a discrete gradient vector field. Thus, from any vertex $v$ there is at most one paired edge $e$ with $(v,e)\in\mathcal{V}$, and hence at most one outgoing edge in $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:acyclic_implies_DAG}
If $\mathcal{V}$ is acyclic in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:acyclic_graph}, then $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ contains no directed cycles.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
A directed cycle $v_0\to v_1\to \cdots \to v_{k-1}\to v_0$ in $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ corresponds exactly to a closed $\mathcal{V}$-path $(v_i,e_i)\in\mathcal{V}$ with $e_i=\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}$, contradicting Definition~\ref{def:acyclic_graph}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{def:anchor_fullgraph}
Assume $\mathcal{V}$ is acyclic. Since $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ is a finite directed graph with outdegree $\le 1$ and no directed cycles (Lemmas~\ref{lem:outdegree_bound}--\ref{lem:acyclic_implies_DAG}), every vertex reaches a terminal sink by iterating outgoing edges. Define the \emph{anchor map} $r:V\to V$ by letting $r(v)$ be the unique sink reached from $v$ in $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Anchors are only needed if one later uses a ``component representative'' tokenization (e.g., anchor tokens). Our main MoMoE split can be implemented using only $(E^{\mathrm{pair}},E^{\mathrm{crit}})$ and does not require anchors.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{def:H0_faithful}
We say $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{$H_0$-faithful} on $G$ if the paired-edge subgraph
\[
P^- := (V,E^{\mathrm{pair}})
\]
induces the same connected-component partition on $V$ as the full graph $G=(V,E)$. Equivalently, for all $u,w\in V$,
\[
u \sim_{P^-} w \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u \sim_G w.
\]
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{def:forested_pairing}
We say $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{forested} if the undirected graph $P^-=(V,E^{\mathrm{pair}})$ is cycle-free (i.e., a forest).
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:H0_vs_forest}
Acyclicity of $\mathcal{V}$ (no closed $\mathcal{V}$-paths) implies $\Gamma(\mathcal{V})$ has no \emph{directed} cycles (Lemma~\ref{lem:acyclic_implies_DAG}), but it does \emph{not} by itself rule out \emph{undirected} cycles in the paired-edge subgraph $P^-$. Thus, to conclude that $P^-$ is a spanning forest one must assume forestedness (Definition~\ref{def:forested_pairing}) in addition to $H_0$-faithfulness.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:cycle_rank_semantic}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph, and let $\mathcal{V}$ be an acyclic discrete gradient vector field on $G$. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal{V}$ is $H_0$-faithful (Definition~\ref{def:H0_faithful}), and
\item $\mathcal{V}$ is forested (Definition~\ref{def:forested_pairing}).
\end{enumerate}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $P^-=(V,E^{\mathrm{pair}})$ is a spanning forest of $G$ (one tree per connected component);
\item consequently,
\[
\beta_1(G)=|E^{\mathrm{crit}}|
\qquad \text{where } E^{\mathrm{crit}}:=E\setminus E^{\mathrm{pair}}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $c$ be the number of connected components of $G$. By $H_0$-faithfulness, $P^-$ has the same component partition as $G$, hence $P^-$ also has $c$ components. By forestedness, each component of $P^-$ is a tree; therefore $|E^{\mathrm{pair}}|=|V|-c$. Now use the standard cycle-rank identity for finite graphs:
\[
\beta_1(G)=|E|-|V|+c.
\]
Since $|E|=|E^{\mathrm{pair}}|+|E^{\mathrm{crit}}|$ and $|E^{\mathrm{pair}}|=|V|-c$, we obtain
\[
\beta_1(G)=(|E^{\mathrm{pair}}|+|E^{\mathrm{crit}}|)-|V|+c  \]\[ = (|V|-c+|E^{\mathrm{crit}}|)-|V|+c =|E^{\mathrm{crit}}|.
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Under the optional strengthened pairing regime of Proposition ~\ref{thm:cycle_rank_semantic}, $A_{\alpha'}$ (paired edges) is a cycle-free connectivity backbone within each component, while $A_{\alpha}$ (critical edges) accounts exactly for the cycle rank ($H_1$ content) of the graph. This supplies a clean semantics for the MoMoE split when one enforces forestedness.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
We assume the reverse kernel $p_\theta(\cdot \mid X_k, \bar{H}, k)$ is Gaussian with covariance $\Sigma_k$ that depends only on the timestep $k$, not on the state $X_k$ or guidance $\bar{H}$. This is standard for DDPM-style diffusion models where $\Sigma_k$ follows a fixed schedule~\cite{ho2020denoising}, but we state it explicitly.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def:skeleton_preserving}
A perturbation $s\mapsto s'$ is \emph{skeleton-preserving} if $\mathrm{Skel}(s')=\mathrm{Skel}(s)$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma:exact_invariance_guidance}
Fix $X^h \in \mathcal{X}$. If $s' \in \mathbb{S}$ is skeleton-preserving relative to $s \in \mathbb{S}$, then $\bar{H}(s') = \bar{H}(s)$. Consequently, for every timestep $k$ and every noised state $X_k$,
\[
    p_\theta(\cdot \mid X_k, \bar{H}(s'), k) = p_\theta(\cdot \mid X_k, \bar{H}(s), k).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We establish the result via the composition chain
\[
    s' \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{Skel}\;}\; \mathrm{Skel}(s') = \mathrm{Skel}(s) \;\xrightarrow{\;\Psi(\cdot, X^h)\;}\; \bar{H}(s') \] \[= \bar{H}(s) \;\xrightarrow{\;p_\theta\;}\; \text{identical distributions}.
\]

By Definition~\ref{def:skeleton_preserving}, the perturbation $s \mapsto s'$ is skeleton-preserving, so $\mathrm{Skel}(s') = \mathrm{Skel}(s)$. Since $\Psi$ is deterministic and the historical input $X^h$ is fixed, it follows that
\[
    \bar{H}(s') = \Psi(\mathrm{Skel}(s'), X^h) = \Psi(\mathrm{Skel}(s), X^h) = \bar{H}(s).
\]
The reverse-step kernel $p_\theta(\cdot \mid X_k, \bar{H}, k)$ is fully determined by the triple $(X_k, \bar{H}, k)$. Since $X_k$ and $k$ are identical in both cases and $\bar{H}(s') = \bar{H}(s)$, the two conditional distributions coincide.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:sufficient_statistic}
Lemma ~\ref{lemma:exact_invariance_guidance} establishes that the Morse skeleton $\mathrm{Skel}(s)$ is a \emph{sufficient characteristic} for the guidance mechanism: any information in the state $s$ that does not affect the skeleton is invisible to the reverse diffusion process. Formally, the guidance  $\bar{H}: \mathbb{S} \to \mathcal{H}$ factors as $\bar{H} = \Psi(\cdot, X^h) \circ \mathrm{Skel}$.
and consequently $\bar{H}(s) = \bar{H}(s')$ whenever $\mathrm{Skel}(s) = \mathrm{Skel}(s')$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:practical_consequences}
We see that under these assumptions that perturbations to edge weights, node features, or auxiliary scores that do not alter the extracted skeleton leave the model's generative distribution unchanged, providing a form of noise robustness. Further, the skeleton acts as an information bottleneck by discarding structural details irrelevant to generation while preserving the topological features that guide the diffusion process.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:scope_limitations}
Theorem~\ref{lemma:exact_invariance_guidance} is, by design, a conditional statement: \emph{if} a perturbation preserves the skeleton, \emph{then} the generative distribution is invariant. The theorem does not address \emph{when} perturbations are skeleton-preserving, nor \emph{how much} the distribution changes when the skeleton does change. In other words, Theorem \ref{lemma:exact_invariance_guidance} does not characterize \emph{which} perturbations are skeleton-preserving. We now develop a quantitative sufficient condition: if a perturbation is small relative to a computable \emph{margin}, the skeleton is guaranteed unchanged.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:decision_representation}
There exist:
\begin{itemize}
    \item a \emph{feature map} $\varphi: \mathbb{S} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ that extracts all scalar quantities examined by the extractor (scores, weights, tie-breaking indices, etc.),
    \item a finite \emph{decision index set} $\mathcal{J}$ enumerating the comparisons performed by the extractor,
    \item for each $j \in \mathcal{J}$, functions $u_j, v_j: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ representing the left and right sides of comparison $j$,
\end{itemize}
such that the extractor output $\mathrm{Skel}(s)$ is fully determined by the sign pattern of the \emph{decision gaps}
\[
    \Delta_j(s) := u_j(\varphi(s)) - v_j(\varphi(s)), \qquad j \in \mathcal{J},
\]
through a deterministic map $F: \{-1, +1\}^{\mathcal{J}} \to Cl(G)$, i.e.,
\[
    \mathrm{Skel}(s) = F\bigl((\mathrm{sign}(\Delta_j(s)))_{j \in \mathcal{J}}\bigr).
\]
We restrict attention to states $s \in \mathcal{S}$ satisfying $\Delta_j(s) \neq 0$ for all $j \in \mathcal{J}$ (the no-ties condition).
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:decision_interpretation}
The feature map $\varphi$ collects all numerical inputs to the extractor into a single vector while the decision index set $\mathcal{J}$ enumerates every comparison the extractor performs. For a sequential pairing algorithm that processes edges in a fixed order and checks Flag variables, this comprises $O(m)$ explicit comparisons: for each edge, one comparison determines endpoint ordering (which vertex has larger score), and the Flag lookup determines the branching outcome. The sequential dependence through Flag variables means that later decisions depend implicitly on earlier ones, but the total number of comparisons remains finite. The functions $u_j$ and $v_j$ extract the quantities being compared: if decision $j$ asks whether $f(v_1) > f(v_2)$, then $u_j(\varphi(s)) = f(v_1)$ and $v_j(\varphi(s)) = f(v_2)$ under state $s$.

The deterministic map $F$ encodes the extractor's logic: once all comparison outcomes (signs) are known, the skeleton is determined. This holds for any algorithm without internal randomness.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:decision_scope}
Assumption~\ref{ass:decision_representation} is satisfied by extractors based on sequential matching, sorting, thresholding, and argmax/argmin operations, since these reduce entirely to pairwise comparisons. The assumption fails for extractors involving continuous optimization (e.g., gradient descent to a local minimum) or soft differentiable relaxations where the output varies smoothly with inputs. 

For the discrete Morse extractor in MG-Diff, vertex scores are assigned based on degree via $g(v) = \deg_{\max} - \deg(v) + \epsilon(v)$ (where $\epsilon(v)$ is a small tie-breaking perturbation) and edges are processed sequentially with a Flag-based construction that determines pairing. Each edge makes a binary decision based on whether its higher-score endpoint is already paired, yielding a finite sequence of comparisons. Assumption~\ref{ass:decision_representation} therefore holds provided tie-breaking is deterministic (e.g., lexicographic ordering on vertex indices). If randomized tie-breakers are used, the analysis applies conditionally on a fixed realization of the random seed.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:no_ties}
The restriction $\Delta_j(s) \neq 0$ for all $j$ excludes states where exact ties occur. This is a genericity assumption: the set of tie-inducing states is small in any reasonable parameterization. In practice, when vertex scores are degree-based, ties occur precisely when two adjacent vertices have identical degree. Such ties can be broken deterministically, which ensures strict inequalities without affecting the topological content of the construction. We state this condition explicitly to avoid degenerate edge cases in the analysis.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:decision_margin}
For a state $s \in \mathbb{S}$ satisfying the no-ties condition, the \emph{decision margin} is
\[
    m(s) := \min_{j \in \mathcal{J}} |\Delta_j(s)|.
\]
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- assumption-2: body_md -->
\label{ass:lipschitz_gaps}
We assume there exists a constant $L_\Delta < \infty$ such that for all $j \in \mathcal{J}$ and all $s, s' \in \mathbb{S}$ if $||\cdot||$ is $l_\infty$,
\[
    |\Delta_j(s') - \Delta_j(s)| \leq L_\Delta \, \|\varphi(s') - \varphi(s)\|.
\]
<!-- end assumption-2 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:lipschitz_verification}
in Assumption ~\ref{ass:lipschitz_gaps} we assert that decision gaps cannot change faster than $L_\Delta$ times the feature displacement, which holds automatically when $u_j$ and $v_j$ are Lipschitz functions of the feature vector.

\paragraph{Why Assumption~\ref{ass:lipschitz_gaps} is reasonable.}
Our extractor is implemented by a finite sequence of comparisons between scalar quantities derived from the input
(e.g., vertex/edge scores, weights, and tie-breaking indices). Each decision gap $\Delta_j$ is a difference of two
such scalars. In our setting these scalars are constructed from bounded-degree algebraic operations
(addition/subtraction, $\min/\max$ over finite sets, and fixed-order sorting/tie-breaking after stable perturbation),
all of which are Lipschitz in $\ell_\infty$ on bounded domains. Consequently each $\Delta_j$ is Lipschitz with some
finite constant, and we may take $L_\Delta:=\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}} L_j$.
When the pipeline includes non-smooth steps (e.g., $\min$), Lipschitz continuity still holds (though not differentiability),
which is exactly what the margin argument requires.


For the MG-Diff extractor in particular, the relevant comparisons are vertex score differences. If we recall that $g(v) = \deg_{\max} - \deg(v) + \varepsilon_v$, the decision gap for an edge $e = \{v_1, v_2\}$ is
\[
    \Delta_j = g(v_1) - g(v_2) = \bigl(\deg(v_2) - \deg(v_1)\bigr) + \bigl(\varepsilon_{v_1} - \varepsilon_{v_2}\bigr),
\]
where the $\deg_{\max}$ terms cancel. So under a perturbation $s \mapsto s'$ that modifies tie-breaker values (degrees are fixed by graph structure), we have
\[
    \Delta_j(s') - \Delta_j(s) = \bigl(\varepsilon'_{v_1} - \varepsilon_{v_1}\bigr) - \bigl(\varepsilon'_{v_2} - \varepsilon_{v_2}\bigr).
\]
Followed by the triangle inequality,
\[
    |\Delta_j(s') - \Delta_j(s)| \leq |\varepsilon'_{v_1} - \varepsilon_{v_1}| + |\varepsilon'_{v_2} - \varepsilon_{v_2}| \leq 2\|\varphi(s') - \] \[ \varphi(s)\|_\infty \leq 2\|\varphi(s') - \varphi(s)\|,
\]
we find that $L_\Delta \leq 2$. This small Lipschitz constant therefore reflects the linear structure of degree-based scoring with additive tie-breakers.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We show that every decision $j \in \mathcal{J}$ has the same sign at $s'$ as at $s$, from which the conclusion follows by determinism of $F$.

Fix an arbitrary $j \in \mathcal{J}$. In view of
the assumptions on decision representations~(\ref{ass:decision_representation}) and Lipschitz conditions~(\ref{ass:lipschitz_gaps}), we obtain
\[
    |\Delta_j(s') - \Delta_j(s)| \leq L_\Delta \, \|\varphi(s') - \varphi(s)\| < L_\Delta \cdot \frac{m(s)}{L_\Delta} = m(s).
\]
By definition of the decision margin, $m(s) = \min_{j' \in \mathcal{J}} |\Delta_{j'}(s)| \leq |\Delta_j(s)|$, so
\[
    |\Delta_j(s') - \Delta_j(s)| < m(s) \leq |\Delta_j(s)|.
\]
This inequality implies that $\Delta_j(s')$ lies strictly within distance $|\Delta_j(s)|$ of $\Delta_j(s)$. Since $\Delta_j(s) \neq 0$ by the no-ties condition, the open interval $(\Delta_j(s) - |\Delta_j(s)|, \Delta_j(s) + |\Delta_j(s)|)$ does not contain zero: if $\Delta_j(s) > 0$, the interval is $(0, 2\Delta_j(s))$, and if $\Delta_j(s) < 0$, the interval is $(2\Delta_j(s), 0)$. In either case, $\Delta_j(s')$ lies in this interval and therefore has the same sign as $\Delta_j(s)$.

Since $j$ was arbitrary, the sign pattern $(\mathrm{sign}(\Delta_j(s')))_{j \in \mathcal{J}}$ equals $(\mathrm{sign}(\Delta_j(s)))_{j \in \mathcal{J}}$. By Assumption~\ref{ass:decision_representation}, $\mathrm{Skel}(s') = F((\mathrm{sign}(\Delta_j(s')))_j) = F((\mathrm{sign}(\Delta_j(s)))_j) = \mathrm{Skel}(s)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:stability_radius}
Theorem~\ref{lem:margin_preserves_skel} defines a \emph{stability radius} around each state:
\[
    r(s) := \frac{m(s)}{L_\Delta}.
\]
Within the open ball $\{s' \in \mathbb{S} : \|\varphi(s') - \varphi(s)\| < r(s)\}$, the skeleton is guaranteed unchanged, and so the generative distribution should remain invariant to local perturbation in this manner.

For the MG-Diff extractor with $L_\Delta \leq 2$, the stability radius is at least $m(s)/2$. If the minimum score gap between adjacent vertices is $\delta > 0$, then perturbations to vertex scores of magnitude less than $\delta/2$ are guaranteed to preserve the skeleton.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:margin_dependence}
The stability guarantee is only as strong as the margin $m(s)$. If the extractor frequently produces near-ties---for instance, when many vertices share the same degree---the margin is small, the stability radius $r(s)$ is correspondingly small, and the guarantee becomes weak. Conversely, if all decisions are made with comfortable gaps, the margin is large and meaningful robustness is assured.

This is not a flaw in the theory but rather an accurate reflection of reality: an extractor operating near decision boundaries \emph{is} sensitive to small perturbations, and the analysis correctly captures this. For degree-based scoring, the margin depends on the degree distribution of the input graph. Graphs with heterogeneous degree sequences yield larger margins than regular or near-regular graphs where many vertices have identical degree.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:lipschitz_role}
The Lipschitz constant $L_\Delta$ appears in the denominator of the stability radius, so a large $L_\Delta$ shrinks the guaranteed stability region. For the MG-Diff extractor based on degree scoring, $L_\Delta \leq 2$ is a small constant arising from the linear structure of coordinate differences. More complex scoring functions (e.g., involving products or nonlinear transformations of features) would yield larger Lipschitz constants and correspondingly weaker stability guarantees.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:computability}
Unlike many stability results in machine learning that provide only existential guarantees, the margin stability framework yields a \emph{computable certificate}. Given a state $s$ and access to the extractor's decision structure, one can enumerate the decision gaps $\{\Delta_j(s)\}_{j \in \mathcal{J}}$, compute $m(s) = \min_j |\Delta_j(s)|$, and obtain an explicit stability radius $r(s) = m(s)/L_\Delta$. For MG-Diff, this amounts to computing the minimum absolute difference $|g(u) - g(v)|$ over all edges $\{u,v\} \in E$, a linear-time operation. This enables post-hoc verification of robustness for individual inputs, a property that may be valuable in safety-critical applications.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:nonidentifiability}
There exists no well-defined map
\[
\Phi:\mathrm{Dgm}_*(\Lambda)\longrightarrow \mathrm{DescMfd}(\Lambda)
\]
from persistence diagrams of filtrations of a finite cell complex $\Lambda$ to descending-manifold structures on $\Lambda$ such that, for every filtration $F$ of $\Lambda$ and every discrete gradient vector field $V$ compatible with $F$, one has
\[
\Phi\big(\mathrm{PH}(F)\big)
\;=\;
\{\mathcal{D}_V(\sigma)\}_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Crit}(V)}.
\]
Equivalently, the fiber over a single persistence diagram may contain filtration-compatible discrete gradient vector fields inducing distinct descending-manifold structures.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The proof follows from the explicit counterexamples constructed below. We exhibit filtrations with genuine finite birth--death intervals and two distinct filtration-compatible gradient vector fields that yield identical persistence diagrams but different descending manifolds.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
Fix an external filtration $F:\Lambda_0\subset\cdots\subset \Lambda_T$ and let $t_F(\sigma)$ denote the first index at which a cell $\sigma$ appears.
A discrete gradient field $\mathcal{V}$ is \emph{entry-time compatible} (with respect to $F$) if every matched pair $(\sigma,\tau)\in\mathcal{V}$ satisfies $t_F(\sigma)=t_F(\tau)$.
Among entry-time compatible matchings, we call $\mathcal{V}$ \emph{maximal} if there is no strictly larger entry-time compatible matching $\mathcal{V}\subsetneq \widetilde{\mathcal{V}}$.
\label{def:max_filtr}
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
Filtration-compatible gradient fields are useful because they yield a smaller filtered Morse complex that computes the same persistence. However, the diagram itself is a property of the filtration, not of the gradient field.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
